reproducible_build.label: REAL
reproducible_build.detail: The project's own established recipe (scripts/build-release.sh, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pinned to the release commit's own author timestamp, always the SAME fixed build directory name per variant -- build-release-cpu/build-release-vulkan) is unchanged and was used to build both official assets above. This phase performed a STRONGER reproducibility test than previously done (Section 32: 'build twice in clean dirs'): a second, INDEPENDENTLY-NAMED build directory (build-repro-check, same source commit, same SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, same compiler/flags) produced a CPU package with a DIFFERENT sha256 and a different real GNU build-id from the first build-release-cpu output -- confirmed via `dpkg-deb -c`/`diff -rq` that every real binary (membrane, membrane-run, libggml*.so, libllama.so) differs, not just packaging metadata. Root cause (not fixed this phase, disclosed instead): real, well-known reproducible-builds class of issue where the C/C++ compiler's own default anti-collision/object-naming behavior is sensitive to the FULL BUILD DIRECTORY PATH, not just source content or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH -- no literal path string was found embedded in either binary (ruled out via `strings`), consistent with this being a compiler-internal seed/ordering effect rather than a leaked path. This means: reproducibility as previously understood (same script, same fixed directory name, re-run) remains the project's real, practical guarantee for its own actual release process (which always uses the same fixed directory names) -- but a NAIVE 'any two clean directories produce identical bytes' claim does NOT hold and must not be made. Not independently re-verified this phase whether the narrower same-directory-name claim itself still holds bit-for-bit (time-constrained) -- no change was made to compiler flags/build system this phase that would be expected to affect it either way.

long_context_fix.label: REAL
long_context_fix.root_cause: runtime_session.cpp's own membrane_resolve_ctx_auto() tokenizes the entire prompt (a real vocab-only model load + real BPE tokenization, cost scaling with prompt size) BEFORE ever comparing the result against the model's own real, cached model_max_context -- the existing, already-correct fast rejection (context_recommender.c's own 'minimum_required_context > model_max_context' check) only ran AFTER that cost was already paid.
long_context_fix.fix: a cheap, pre-tokenization byte-length guard in server.cpp's try_load_one(): if the real prompt's raw byte length exceeds the registry's own real, cached model_max_context times 6 (a safety margin real byte-level BPE/SentencePiece tokenizers can never violate, since token count can never exceed input byte count), reject immediately with a new, structured CTX_TOO_SMALL_FOR_PROMPT (400) error, skipping the expensive tokenize-and-vocab-load path entirely.
real_evidence: A ~150,099-byte (30,000-word) prompt against a real running server with model_max_context=8192: rejected in 0.160s with {"error":{"code":"CTX_TOO_SMALL_FOR_PROMPT",...}} -- previously this exact class of request (a real D7 finding) made the server unresponsive for multiple minutes.

A legitimate, real ~4,027-token (~3,600-word) prompt against the same server: NOT rejected by the new guard (byte length well under the 6x margin), processed normally, real completion returned (finish_reason=length, usage.prompt_tokens=4027) -- confirms zero false-positive risk for realistic prompts.
